etymology: A river, or a canal and the district about it, in Babylonia, where Ezra gathered the returning exiles and proclaimed a fast before the journey to Jerusalem; the name’s meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: The river of Ahava was a stream, or a canal and the region about it, in Babylonia, where Ezra assembled the company of exiles who would return with him to Jerusalem. “I gathered them together to the river that runneth to Ahava; and there abode we in tents three days”. There, before setting out on the long and dangerous road, Ezra did a memorable thing: “Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance” (Ezr 8:21). He tells us plainly why he did not ask the king for an escort: “I was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy in the way: because we had spoken unto the king, saying, The hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him” (Ezr 8:22). Having confessed God as his protector, Ezra would not then lean on the arm of flesh; he fasted and prayed, and God heard, and brought the company safely home with all their treasure. The river of Ahava thus preaches the seeking of God rather than the powers of the world: it is no shame to trust the LORD and refuse the props of the flesh, for the hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek Him. He that has professed dependence on God must live it, and shall not be put to shame.
webster_summary: A river in Babylonia where Ezra fasted and sought God’s protection for the journey home rather than the king’s soldiers; a lesson in trusting God over the arm of flesh.

etymology: A river, or canal, by the palace of Shushan in the province of Elam, on whose bank Daniel received his vision of the ram and the he-goat; the name is of Persian origin.
biblical_def: The river Ulai was a stream, or broad canal, by the palace of Shushan in the province of Elam, on whose bank the prophet Daniel stood in vision. “I saw in a vision, and I was by the river of Ulai” (Dan 8:2); and there he beheld the ram with two horns and the rough he-goat, and heard the interpreting angel: “I heard a man’s voice between the banks of Ulai, which called, and said, Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision” (Dan 8:16). By the Ulai, God unveiled to Daniel the rise and fall of the empires yet to come — the ram, the kings of Media and Persia; the he-goat, the king of Greece; the little horn that would magnify himself against the Prince of the host. Centuries before these kingdoms arose, God set their course in a vision by a Persian river, that His people might know that history is not a blind tumult but the unrolling of a decree. The river Ulai thus stands as a monument to the certainty of prophecy and the sovereignty of God over the nations. He declares the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand. The believer, watching the empires of his own day rise and fall, rests in the God who told Daniel by the Ulai what should be, and whose kingdom alone shall never be destroyed.

etymology: A river, and the region about it, in Mesopotamia, one of the places to which the ten tribes of Israel were carried captive by Assyria; the name is taken to mean “quarry” or “cutting off.”
biblical_def: The river Gozan, and the district about it, in Mesopotamia, was one of the places of exile to which Assyria carried the ten tribes of Israel. “In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes” (2Ki 17:6). This was the end of the northern kingdom, and the Scripture is careful to tell us why: it came “because they had not obeyed the voice of the LORD their God, but transgressed his covenant”. The captivity by the river Gozan is the sober monument of a nation that forsook the LORD, went after other gods, and would not hear the prophets He sent early and late; and at the last He removed them out of His sight. Yet even in this judgment mercy is not wholly hid. God had a remnant according to the election of grace even in apostate Israel; and the prophets who foretold the scattering foretold also a gathering, when the LORD would set His hand again to recover the remnant of His people. The river Gozan warns every generation of the deadly seriousness of forsaking the covenant, and of a God who will by no means clear the guilty; yet it stands within the larger story of a covenant-keeping God who will not utterly cast off, but preserves and gathers a remnant to Himself.

etymology: One of the two rivers of Damascus, named by Naaman the Syrian leper when he despised the prophet’s command to wash in Jordan; the name is taken to mean “swift” or “rushing.”
biblical_def: Pharpar was one of the two rivers of Damascus, named in the account of Naaman the Syrian leper. When the prophet Elisha bade him go wash seven times in the Jordan and be clean, Naaman was wroth, both at the plainness of the cure and at the choice of so mean a river: “Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean?” (2Ki 5:12). To his proud eye, the clear rivers of his own city were nobler than the muddy Jordan, and the whole business beneath his dignity. So he turned away in a rage, and would have gone home a leper still, but that his servants reasoned him into obedience: if the prophet had bidden some great thing, would he not have done it? how much rather, then, wash and be clean. He humbled himself, went down into the despised Jordan, and came up whole. The river Pharpar stands for the pride that despises God’s appointed way of cleansing and prefers its own. Men still say, in effect, Are not the waters of my own choosing better? — preferring their own works, their own reason, their own religion to the one simple, humbling way God has set. But there is cleansing in no river but the one God appoints; the leprosy of sin is washed away only in the blood of Christ, and only by those who will stoop to the humbling gospel and obey.

etymology: A mountain on the northern border of Judah, also called Chesalon; the name means “mount of forests” or “mountain of woods.” Not to be confounded with the city Kirjath-jearim.
biblical_def: Mount Jearim was a wooded height on the northern border of Judah, also called Chesalon. It is named in the tracing of Judah’s bound: “the border compassed from Baalah westward unto mount Seir, and passed along unto the side of mount Jearim, which is Chesalon, on the north side” (Jos 15:10). The name means mount of forests, or mountain of woods, from the trees that clothed its slopes. It is not to be confounded with the city Kirjath-jearim, the city of forests, that lay in the same wooded region. A forest-clad mountain of the border turns the mind to the great Scriptural theme of creation’s praise: for the woods and the trees are called, again and again, to rejoice before the LORD their Maker. “Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice before the LORD” (Psa 96:12-13), for He cometh to judge the earth. The mountains and hills break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field clap their hands. A mount of forests is a natural choir, its every tree a witness to the wisdom and goodness of the Creator, and a summons to man, the crown of creation, to lead the praise that the very woods offer. Mount Jearim, obscure as a border-mark, stands as a green pulpit whence the trees of the wood rejoice before the LORD, and rebuke the silence of a man who will not praise his Maker.

etymology: A promontory and town on the western coast of Asia Minor, opposite Samos, where Paul’s ship tarried on his voyage to Jerusalem; a stopping-place on the apostle’s third journey.
biblical_def: Trogyllium was a promontory and small town on the western coast of Asia Minor, opposite the island of Samos, where Paul’s ship put in for a night on his last voyage toward Jerusalem. “We came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus” (Act 20:15). It is one of the many stages Luke sets down in the careful log of that journey, as Paul pressed on toward Jerusalem to keep the feast, though he knew that bonds and afflictions awaited him. At Miletus, the next stop, he would call the elders of Ephesus and take his farewell, telling them, “I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there…But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy” (Act 20:22-24). Trogyllium, a night’s anchorage, is thus a small waymark in a great resolve: the ordered steps of a servant set on finishing the work his Lord had given him. It teaches the believer that the way of obedience is walked one stage at a time, from Chios to Samos to Trogyllium to Miletus, each step ordered of God and each bringing the servant nearer to the cross he is called to bear, and to the crown that lies beyond it.

etymology: A harbor on the south coast of Crete which Paul’s ship sought to reach for the winter, but was driven past by the storm; not to be confused with Phenice (Phoenicia), the coastland north of Galilee.
biblical_def: Phenice was a harbor on the south coast of Crete, a haven that the sailors of Paul’s ship hoped to reach and there to winter. “Because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence also, if by any means they might attain to Phenice, and there to winter” (Act 27:12). Paul had warned them not to sail, foretelling loss and danger; but the counsel of the centurion and the shipmaster prevailed, and they weighed anchor for Phenice, only a little way along the coast. They never reached it. Scarcely had they set out when a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon, seized the ship and drove her helpless before it for many days, until all hope of being saved was taken away, and at last they were wrecked upon Malta. The harbor of Phenice, so near and so confidently sought, stands as a lasting parable that man proposes but God disposes. “A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). The sailors devised to winter comfortably at Phenice; God had appointed instead a storm, a shipwreck, and a strange island, that Paul might preach there and that the mercy of God might be shown to all aboard. The believer learns from Phenice not to lean on his own plans, however reasonable, but to commit his way to the LORD, who often withholds the near harbor to bring His people, by a harder road, to a better end than they had devised.

etymology: A small island off the south coast of Crete, called Clauda in the Authorized Version, under whose lee Paul’s storm-driven ship found brief shelter to secure the boat; the name is of local origin.
biblical_def: Cauda, called Clauda in the Authorized Version, was a small island off the south coast of Crete, remembered for a moment of brief respite in the great storm that carried Paul toward shipwreck. When the tempestuous wind Euroclydon had seized the ship and was driving her helplessly, they came for a little while under the shelter of this island: “running under a certain island which is called Clauda, we had much work to come by the boat” (Act 27:16). In the island’s lee, out of the worst of the wind for a short space, the sailors were able to haul in the ship’s boat, undergird the vessel with cables, and make what preparation they could before being driven out again into the open storm. Cauda is thus a small mercy in a great danger — a brief calm granted in the midst of the tempest, that the crew might do the necessary work of the moment before the wind took them again. So God deals with His people in their storms: He seldom removes the tempest all at once, but grants breathing-spaces, lees and shelters along the way, brief calms in which to gather strength and make ready for what is yet to come. The believer, tossed in the storms of this life, learns from Cauda to seize the small mercies God gives in the lulls, and to trust that the same hand which sheltered the ship a little while will bring it, through all the storm, to the shore He has appointed.

corruption_summary: An island of Scripture giving brief shelter in the storm; it recovers the truth that God grants small mercies and breathing-spaces to His people amid great trials.
corruption_paragraphs: Cauda faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth its shelter carries answers both the despair that sees only the unbroken fury of the storm and the ingratitude that overlooks the small mercies and brief calms God grants in the midst of trouble.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God’s mercy in the storm. He seldom stills the tempest all at once, but grants lees and shelters like Cauda, brief calms in which His people may gather strength and make ready. The believer seizes the small mercies given in the lulls, trusting the hand that sheltered the ship a little while to bring it, through the whole storm, to the appointed shore.

etymology: An island of the Aegean Sea, off the coast of Asia Minor, at which Paul’s ship touched on his voyage toward Jerusalem; spelled Coos in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Cos, spelled Coos in the Authorized Version, was an island of the Aegean Sea off the coast of Asia Minor, one of the stages of Paul’s last voyage toward Jerusalem. After the sorrowful parting from the elders of Ephesus at Miletus, Luke records the daily run of the ship: “it came to pass, that after we were gotten from them, and had launched, we came with a straight course unto Coos, and the day following unto Rhodes, and from thence unto Patara” (Act 21:1). Cos was a night’s anchorage on a straight and prosperous run, one link in the chain of ports that carried the apostle nearer to the city where bonds awaited him. The very ordinariness of the notice is instructive: the servant of God is borne along, day by day, port by port, by winds and providences he does not govern, yet all working to set him where God would have him. Even the straight course and fair wind to Cos were of the Lord, who orders the seas and the ways of His servants. The island stands, like Trogyllium and Rhodes and Patara, as a small witness that no stage of a believer’s journey is outside the ordering of God: the smooth days as well as the storms, the fair winds as well as the foul, are all appointed to bring the servant to his place and his work. The Lord directeth the steps, and the sea-miles, of them that are His.
webster_summary: An Aegean island where Paul’s ship touched on his way to Jerusalem; a witness that God orders every stage of His servants’ journey, the fair days as well as the storms.

etymology: A rugged, mountainous region of Asia Minor which Paul and Barnabas crossed with the gospel on the first missionary journey; distinct from the city of Antioch in Pisidia, which lay upon its border.
biblical_def: Pisidia was a rugged and mountainous region of Asia Minor, a wild highland country of steep passes and lurking robbers, which Paul and Barnabas traversed with the gospel on the first missionary journey. It is to be distinguished from the city of Antioch in Pisidia, which stood upon its border. Returning from the coast to strengthen the young churches, “after they had passed throughout Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia” (Act 14:24), preaching the word in Perga as they went. This region was among the most dangerous of the apostle’s travels; it is likely of such highland crossings that Paul wrote when he numbered his sufferings for the gospel: “in journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers…in perils in the wilderness…in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst” (2Co 11:26-27). To carry the gospel through Pisidia was to hazard life and limb among the mountains for the sake of Christ and His church. The region thus stands as a witness to the cost of the gospel’s spread: it was not borne to the nations by ease and comfort, but through perils, hardship, and toil, by men who counted not their lives dear. The believer, tempted to shrink from any small hardship in the Lord’s service, remembers Pisidia, and the apostles who crossed its dangerous heights that the churches might be planted and the word of life carried through.

The truth its dangerous heights carry answers the soft assumption that the gospel spreads by ease and comfort, forgetting the perils, hardships, and toil by which it was actually borne to the nations.
